How to learn words so they stay in your head

Learning more words is not the same as speaking. Here is how to learn words in context, use them in your own sentences, and review them before they fade.

Published April 5, 2024 · 7 min read · Sławomir Onyszko ·Updated November 14, 2026

A long word list feels like progress. You add another word, another flashcard, and the list grows. Then you want to say a sentence about your job, and the word is not there.

That does not mean the list is useless. It means the list is only the beginning. A word you only recognize is not yet a word you can use.

Knowing a word is three things

Knowing a word means you can recognize it, understand it, and use it in your own sentence. Those are three levels. A list helps with the first. Context helps with the second. Only your own sentence shows whether the word is really yours.

You might recognize "aunque" when you read it. That does not mean you can say "Aunque estaba cansado, terminé la lección" without pausing. Recognition is passive vocabulary. Speaking needs active vocabulary, the ability to use the word yourself.

A word you only recognize is like a tool behind a shop window. You know what it looks like. You still cannot use it.

Words stick when they are useful to you

Words are easier to remember when they do something for you. A word you need to describe your work, your family, or your weekend has a job. A word from a random list of rare adjectives does not.

Start with words you meet often and words you need. If you read a story about cooking, learn the words for the actions in that story. If you talk about your job, learn the words you keep reaching for. Frequency matters, but whether the word is useful to you matters more.

Context gives a word a frame

A word in a sentence has neighbors. Those neighbors give it meaning and make it easier to remember. "Pedir prestado" is easier to remember in "¿Puedo pedir prestado tu bolígrafo?" than in a list next to "prestar".

When you read a short story, notice the words that repeat or block your understanding. Do not stop for every word. Finish the story first. Then go back to a few words that seem useful.

Write the word with the sentence you found it in. Add the meaning in your own words, not a dictionary definition you do not understand. If the word has a pattern, note it. "Pedir prestado" goes with an object from a person. "Prestar" goes the other way.

Your own sentence turns a word into a skill

Write one sentence about your life with the word. Then say it out loud. If you can, record it. That is the moment when the word stops being only recognized.

Example: you learn "aunque". Write: "Aunque estaba cansado, terminé la lección." Then say it. Then change it: "Aunque estaba cansado, llamé a mi amigo." The second sentence is yours. That is the one that will stick.

Ask for a correction if you have someone to ask: a tutor, a language exchange partner, or an app. A correction tells you what a more natural version is and why.

Active recall works better than re-reading

Instead of reading a flashcard again, try to remember the word before you look at the answer. It is harder, and that is why it works. Your brain practices retrieving the word, not just recognizing it.

Connect the new word to something you already know: an image, a sound, your own experience, or a sentence about yourself. A word that is about you is easier to keep. For example, you can connect "pedir prestado" to the time you borrowed a book from a friend.

This is memory built on associations, not on repeating a list. The more paths that lead to a word, the easier it is to find it when you speak.

Review before the word disappears

Review is not the same as re-reading. Re-reading feels familiar, but familiarity is not recall. You need to retrieve the word from memory.

Spaced repetition means you review a word when you are about to forget it. If it is easy, it comes back later. If it is hard, it comes back sooner. The system chooses when to bring the word back.

In Soliloquy, words from stories, corrections from speaking, and phrases you practice go into one deck. You do not have to build cards or track due dates yourself. The app decides what is due today.

A 15-minute word session

  1. Read a short story at your level. The story is optional, but it gives you context.
  2. Pick a few words that repeat or block your understanding.
  3. Write one sentence with each word about your own life.
  4. Say the sentences out loud and record one.
  5. Save the words and your corrections to one deck.
  6. Review what is due today.

The session is short on purpose. A few words you can use are worth more than a long list you only recognize.

Words come alive in conversation

You can learn words alone, but a real conversation shows whether you can use them under time pressure. Language exchange, meetups, and online groups give you another person.

Prepare 3 topics you want to talk about. Meet regularly, even for a short time. Do not expect the first conversation to be perfect. A word used in conversation sticks differently from a word on a flashcard.

When words disappear

It is normal to forget half of the new words after a week. That does not mean the method is broken. Forgetting is part of learning, and review is there to bring the word back.

Sometimes progress slows down and a few weeks feel harder. Change the material, go back to your reason, and make the goal smaller. You do not have to do more every day.

Common traps

  • Translating every word in a story. You lose the meaning and remember the translation, not the scene.
  • Collecting flashcards without reviewing them. A deck you never open is not practice.
  • Learning rare words before useful ones. A rare word you cannot use is not an achievement.
  • Ignoring pronunciation. A word you cannot say is hard to use in a conversation.

How many words should you learn?

There is no universal number. It depends on your level, your time, and what you need the language for. A fixed quota can push you to collect words instead of using them.

A better question is: how many words can you use in a short answer this week? If you learn a few words and use them in your own sentences, you are doing more for your speaking than if you memorize a list.

Hard questions

Can I learn words in isolation?

Yes, for recognition. But if you want to speak, you need context and your own sentences. A flashcard with a word and a translation is a start, not the whole job.

How long does it take to learn a word?

It depends on the word, your level, and how often you use it. Some words stick after a few encounters. Others need many reviews. There is no single number that fits everyone.

How many words a day?

There is no universal number either. Start with a small batch you can use in sentences. Increase it only if you can still keep up with review and use the words in sentences.

Do I need someone to talk to?

No. You can start alone. A tutor or a language exchange partner helps later for real conversation, but daily speaking and review can be done on your own.

Make one word yours

Pick one word you would need today. Write a sentence about yourself with it, say it out loud, and save a flashcard. That is enough for today.
